activities.anchor: at every point between the Roman Empire and the Ming
activities.caption: call the band — the Malthusian ceiling
activities.name: econBandEstimate

config.prompt: In Angus Maddison's estimates, average incomes drifted inside a narrow band for millennia. Roughly how many international dollars a year did that band sit around?
config.why: Anywhere from about 450 to 600 international dollars — for millennia: better harvests made more mouths, not more comfort, and the variable that moved was population, not welfare.

activities.caption: drag the divider — the trap and the wage islands
activities.name: econIslandsCompare

config.prompt: Flat living standards — with exceptions that mattered — drag the divider:

before.label: the trap
before.text: Wages oscillating around subsistence, occasional crises — harvest failures, epidemics — doing the correcting. Living standards flat, not death constant: most of the time the mechanism worked gently.

after.label: the wage islands
after.text: Late-medieval England and the early-modern Netherlands built real wages above subsistence — precisely the clue later economists used to find the exit.

config.why: In the Malthusian world the student's question is not 'were they poor?' but 'what reset the balance?' — plague, new crops, or, once, a machine.

activities.anchor: which does not sound dramatic until compounding is done
activities.caption: run the compounding — one per cent, doubled
activities.name: econCompoundingEstimate

config.prompt: Industrialising Britain grew income per head at around 1 per cent a year. At that rate, income doubles in roughly how many years?
config.why: About 70 — a rate that looks trivial rewrites material life within two generations; the century after 1830 multiplied British real output per head several times over.
config.context: Before 1800, growth of income per head across the world economy was close to zero — perhaps a few hundredths of a per cent a year.

activities.anchor: what Britain uniquely offered was a
activities.caption: bet before you read on — endogenous inventions
activities.name: econEndogenousPredict

config.q: The lesson calls inventions 'endogenous'. What does that mean?
choices: They are produced by lone geniuses working in isolation
They arrive where the price system calls for them, financed by institutions that reward them
They were imported ready-made from China and India
config.why: Spinning wheels, silk machinery and steam toys existed in China, India and France — what Britain offered was a payoff to mechanising: wages high, energy cheap, patent protection from 1624, financiers ready.

activities.anchor: The wage evidence is the sharpest instrument
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the divergence debate
activities.name: econWageSpot

config.prompt: One line of this Great Divergence summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Pomeranz (2000) argued the Yangzi delta was broadly comparable to England as late as the mid-eighteenth century.
Europe's escape came partly from luck: accessible coal and the New World's land, sugar and cotton.
Real-wage comparisons suggest northwest Europe pulled ahead by the seventeenth or early eighteenth century.
Construction workers in London and Amsterdam earned about the same as unskilled workers in Delhi or Beijing.
If divergence was late and contingent, convergence is possible and normal.
config.correction: Allen's comparative series show London and Amsterdam construction workers earning several times what unskilled workers in Delhi or Beijing took home in the eighteenth century.
config.why: A gap wide enough to make labour-saving machinery rational on one side of Eurasia and pointless on the other — and the answer has moved with every dataset the Maddison Project and its rivals have built.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the slavery-and-cotton ledger
activities.name: econCottonCloze

config.text: Eric Williams made his thesis in %%0%%; the slave trade was abolished in %%1%% at a moment of profitability, not decline; and around %%2%% of Britain's raw cotton in the 1850s came from the American South — the plantation system underwriting the factory system.
config.hint: The direct-finance version of the thesis looks overstated; the cotton channel looks understated.

activities.anchor: The anthropometric evidence is the pessimists
activities.caption: pair each witness with its testimony
activities.name: econOptimistsMatch

config.prompt: The standard-of-living debate — pair each piece of evidence with its side:

pairs.right: wages roughly flat from the 1780s to the 1820s while hours and crowding worsened
measurably shorter than those born generations earlier
a Manchester labourer's average age at death: 17, against rural levels near 40

config.why: The gains were real — but they arrived late, unevenly, and only where public health and politics caught up with productivity.

activities.anchor: share an anatomy economists now recognise
activities.caption: line up the crashes, earliest first
activities.name: econCrashOrder

config.prompt: Eight centuries of manias — order these by year, earliest first:
items: The panic that began with Vienna's stock exchange — 1873
config.why: Reinhart and Rogoff's database of eight centuries made the pattern quantitative: sovereign defaults cluster, banking crises are roughly as old as banks — and 1873 became the first genuinely global downturn, while after 1929 American shares fell nearly 90 per cent by 1932.
